extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and general readers seeking an overview of the legal doctrine of standing (locus standi)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the legal standards and jurisdictional variations that determine whether a party has standing (locus standi) to bring a case. Covers core Article III elements, prudential limits, and country-specific tests and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: General definition of standing (locus standi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing or locus standi is a condition that a party seeking a legal remedy must show they have, by demonstrating to the court sufficient connection to and harm from the law or action challenged to support that party's participation in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article opens by explaining standing as the basic requirement that a party have 'something to lose'—a sufficient connection and harm—so the court may adjudicate the dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations in which a party has standing (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party has standing in the following situations: (1) The party is directly subject to an adverse effect by the statute or action and the harm will continue unless the court grants relief; (2) The party will be directly harmed by the conditions for which they are asking relief; (3) The party is not directly harmed but the harm has a reasonable relation to their situation (e.g., First Amendment 'chilling effects'); (4) The party is granted automatic standing by act of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list (from the article's lead) provides alternative bases for standing including direct injury, imminent injury, third-party or chilling-effect interests, and statutory/automatic grants of standing (with examples such as environmental statutes allowing suits and statutory attorney-fee shifting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III justiciability / case-or-controversy limitation (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts require a 'case or controversy' under Article III of the Constitution; the litigant must be entitled to have the court decide the merits. Courts will not issue advisory opinions and will only hear mature, justiciable disputes with a tangible interest at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle limits federal judicial power and is the constitutional foundation for the injury/causation/redressability tests discussed below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injury-in-fact (Article III requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must have suffered or imminently will suffer injury—an invasion of a legally protected interest that is (a) concrete and particularized, and (b) actual or imminent (neither conjectural nor hypothetical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injury-in-fact may be economic or non-economic. The injury must be personal to the party seeking review ('the party seeking review be himself among the injured'). The Lujan and related cases emphasize imminence and concreteness (e.g., speculative or programmatic harms often fail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation (Article III requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a causal connection between the injury and the conduct complained of, so that the injury is fairly traceable to the challenged action of the defendant and not the result of the independent action of some third party who is not before the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for a sufficiently direct nexus between defendant conduct and plaintiff injury; overly attenuated chains of causation (as in Allen v. Wright) may defeat standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redressability (Article III requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be likely, as opposed to merely speculative, that a favorable court decision will redress the injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a court cannot provide relief that will remedy the plaintiff's injury, redressability is lacking. Lujan and other decisions analyze whether invalidation of the challenged action would actually ameliorate the plaintiff's asserted injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudential limitation — general prohibition on third-party standing
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may only assert their own rights and cannot raise the claims of a third party who is not before the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions exist where the third party has interchangeable economic interests with the injured party, where a 'next friend' can represent an infant or ward, or where statute provides an exception (e.g., qui tam relators under the False Claims Act). Congress may override prudential limits by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudential limitation — prohibition of generalized grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff cannot sue if the alleged injury is widely shared in an undifferentiated way with many people (generalized grievance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the general rule against federal taxpayer standing; such grievances are ordinarily for the representative branches rather than the courts. Some narrow exceptions exist at state or municipal levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudential limitation — zone of interest test
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff must fall within the 'zone of interest' protected by the statute or constitutional provision at issue; relatedly, courts consider the 'zone of injury'—whether the injury is the kind Congress expected to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The zone-of-interest inquiry is used to assess whether the plaintiff's interests are arguably among those the statute was meant to protect; it can bar suits by plaintiffs outside that statutory interest even when Article III standing elements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest standing (Canada — Standing trilogy formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When public interest standing is sought, three aspects are considered: (1) is there a serious issue raised as to the invalidity of the legislation; (2) has it been established that the plaintiff is directly affected by the legislation or, if not, does the plaintiff have a genuine interest in its validity; (3) is there another reasonable and effective way to bring the issue before the court?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the Supreme Court of Canada's 'Standing trilogy' and summarized in Canadian Council of Churches v. Canada; public-interest standing can also be available in non‑constitutional cases (Finlay v. Canada).

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian common-law and statutory tests for standing
rubrics_metrics.description: At common law the test is whether the plaintiff has a 'special interest in the subject matter of the action'. Under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977, to have standing the applicant must be 'a person who is aggrieved' (defined as 'a person whose interests are adversely affected').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Australian law generally does not recognize open standing unless statute allows it; courts inquire into remoteness and whether the plaintiff is specially affected compared with the public at large. Prerogative writs have a lower standing burden; Attorneys General have presumed standing in administrative law; amicus curiae participation is recognised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest and class standing (Australia — representative aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing may apply to a class of aggrieved people where closeness of the plaintiff to the subject matter is decisive; plaintiff must show they have been specially affected in comparison with the public at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures how Australian courts treat group or public interest litigants and emphasizes the need to show a special or particular concern rather than a general grievance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nigeria: traditional vs liberal approaches to locus standi
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional approach: only a party who has suffered pecuniary or special damage can seek redress. Liberal approach: locus standi may be granted more broadly, allowing any person subject to the constitution to challenge unconstitutionality or infringement of fundamental human rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nigerian jurisprudence has examples and case citations showing movement from strict damage-based locus standi toward broader constitutional standing in certain contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: England & Wales — 'sufficient interest' for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant for judicial review must have a sufficient interest in the matter; the courts have construed 'sufficient interest' liberally to allow public-spirited litigants (pressure groups, taxpayers) to vindicate the rule of law in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Diplock emphasized avoiding lacunae that would prevent public-spirited parties or single taxpayers from bringing matters to court. The doctrine of privity in contract and statutory modifications (Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999) also affect who may sue in contract contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to challenge statutes — general rule and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, a party cannot have standing to challenge a statute's constitutionality unless they will be subjected to the statute's provisions. Exceptions exist (e.g., First Amendment overbreadth/chilling-effect challenges) and when the statute's existence would deprive someone of a right or privilege (the 'something to lose' principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: First Amendment overbreadth permits a partially affected person to challenge other parts of the statute because of chilling effects on speech. The Martin v. Ziherl example shows standing where a person would lose a substantive right (ability to sue) if a statute were upheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxpayer standing (United States and state variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal taxpayer standing is generally insufficient to establish Article III standing because federal conduct is too remote from individual taxpayer returns; however, exceptions exist (e.g., municipal taxpayer suits), and some states recognize broader taxpayer actions (California, Florida, Virginia have state-specific rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Frothingham and later cases (e.g., DaimlerChrysler v. Cuno) and notes state statutory and case-law variations where taxpayers may sue to prevent illegal expenditures or waste of public funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to challenge federal contract awards (interested party test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only an 'interested party' has standing to challenge a federal contract award — defined as a company or person who bid for a contract, or a prospective bidder, whose 'direct economic interest would be affected by the award of the contract' to another business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative contract‑appeal forums and boards apply this direct‑economic‑interest test (example: District of Columbia Contracts Appeals Board limiting standing to protestors who would be in line for award).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing of ballot-measure proponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Being proponents of a ballot measure is not by itself enough to confer legal standing (Hollingsworth v. Perry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents must show they are directly harmed or otherwise meet standing requirements; merely sponsoring or supporting a measure does not automatically create an Article III interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-law variation and forum-specific doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: State standing doctrines differ substantially from federal law and vary from state to state; some states focus on whether the plaintiff has pleaded a cause of action rather than applying a federal-style Article III standing analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: California example: courts emphasize whether the plaintiff has sufficiently pleaded a cause of action; the legal term 'standing' is sometimes conflated with jus tertii and treated differently under state law and procedure (e.g., California taxpayer actions, local rules).
